newsitem.title: TURKEY: Amoco suggests Turkey buy gas from Egypt not others.
newsitem.headline: Amoco suggests Turkey buy gas from Egypt not others.

text.p: U.S. oil giant Amoco has suggested Turkey look to Egyptian natural gas sources to replace a multi-billion-dollar project to get gas supplies from Iran through a pipeline, a senior company official said.

"Egypt is a stronger and better alternative for gas supplies to Turkey than others," said Richard Flury, Amoco's executive vice president, referring to Turkey's $23-billion agreement with Iran to get gas through a pipeline from Iran's Tabriz to the Turkish capital.

In his comments to reporters at an introductory meeting in Ankara on Thursday night of his company's partnership with other world energy companies and a Turkish group, he said his company would be committed to bringing LNG to Turkey from Egypt under a joint venture with Italy's Eni and Total of France.
The Amoco-led partnership, which includes Eni, Total, Japan's energy firm Mitsui & Co and Turkish conglomerate Yasar Holding, has been formed to bid in several energy projects in Turkey, he said.
"This wide-ranging and international consortium has agreed to combine their technical, commercial and financial expertise to contribute to the development of Turkey," he said.
"The partnership is committed to help solve Turkey's energy problem," he said. He did not give other details.

But Mick Jarvis, general manager of the London-based Amoco International Gas Development Ltd, an Amoco subsidiary, said the partnership, which has already bid for an LNG re-gasification plant and gas-fired power plant next to it in western Turkey, was considering other projects in Turkey.
The consortium participated in a government tender in February to build two 700-Megawatt (MW) power plants in the western town of Aliaga for a price tag between $1 to $1.5 billion.
The government tendered in February for four other gas-fired plants in several other locations, all of them worth about $5 billion.

Turkey, which has an annual energy shortage of about 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 1997, is trying to lessen dependence on oil and coal for energy sources and has been using Russian gas and Algerian LNG for industrial and domestic use.
"We want to be involved in a similar power plant project in Iskenderun and some pipeline projects in Turkey," Jarvis told Reuters. He did not elaborate on the projects.
"We also have a project to bring Egyptian gas to Turkey in LNG form. Bringing gas through a pipeline from Egypt under the sea is more expensive so we don't want that option," he said.
He said using LNG gave flexibility for power plants in terms of supply and demand.
The other contenders for the Aliaga project include consortia involving Mobil, Marubeni of Japan, Enron, Russian Gazprom GAZP.RTS, General Electric and local contractors.
Jarvis said they had a better chance of winning the tender because of their pledge to supply gas.
"We have the advantage of bringing gas to Turkey from Egypt," he said.
